rows.stem: A compound undergoes complete dimerization in a given organic solvent. The Van't Hoff factor 'i' is :
rows.solution:
The van't Hoff factor is \(0{\cdot}5\).

That factor compares the number of particles ACTUALLY present with the number the formula predicts:
\(i = \dfrac{\text{observed number of particles}}{\text{expected number of particles}}\)

DIMERIZATION means two molecules combine into one, and COMPLETE dimerization means every molecule does so. Two particles dissolved therefore become ONE:
\(i = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0{\cdot}5\)

A value BELOW 1 is the signature of ASSOCIATION, and every colligative property is halved with it — the freezing point depression, the boiling point elevation and the osmotic pressure are each half what the formula would predict.

Benzoic acid in benzene is the standard case, its two molecules held together by a pair of hydrogen bonds between their carboxyl groups. A value of \(2{\cdot}0\) would mean DISSOCIATION into two ions, the opposite situation and the trap in the question.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: For the reaction \(\mathrm{A} + 2\mathrm{B} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}\), the rate law is given by \(\mathrm{r} = \mathrm{k[A]\,[B]^{2}}\), the concentration of A is kept constant while that of B is doubled. The rate of the reaction will :
rows.solution:
The rate becomes FOUR TIMES its original value.

The rate law is \(r = k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2\), and the concentration of A is held constant, so only the second factor changes. Doubling \([\mathrm{B}]\) multiplies that factor by \(2^2\):
\(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = \left(\dfrac{2[\mathrm{B}]}{[\mathrm{B}]}\right)^{2} = 4\)

The EXPONENT is what matters, not the coefficient in the equation — although here they happen to agree, both being 2. Order is measured experimentally and need not match the stoichiometry at all, so the rate law must be read rather than the equation.

Had the order in B been 1, the rate would merely have doubled; had it been zero, nothing would have changed.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
The interstitial compounds of transition metals are
than the metal itself.
rows.solution:
Interstitial compounds are HARDER than the metal itself.

They form when small atoms — hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, boron — occupy the INTERSTICES, the empty spaces between the metal atoms in the crystal lattice. They are usually non-stoichiometric, with formulae such as \(\mathrm{TiC}\) or \(\mathrm{Fe_3H}\).

The trapped atoms make it harder for one layer of metal atoms to SLIDE over another, and that sliding is what makes a pure metal soft and malleable. Blocking it makes the material hard and brittle.

Steel is the everyday example: carbon atoms in the interstices of iron give a material far harder and stronger than pure iron, which is soft.

Two further properties follow, and they can seem contradictory. Interstitial compounds retain METALLIC CONDUCTIVITY, since the metal's own electron sea is undisturbed, but they lose DUCTILITY and MALLEABILITY, since those depend on the sliding that is now blocked. Their melting points are also higher than the parent metal's.

rows.stem:
What type of isomerism is shown by the following pair of complex compounds ?
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]\,[Cr(CN)_6]}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]\,[Co(CN)_6]}\)
rows.solution:
The pair shows COORDINATION ISOMERISM.

This isomerism needs a compound in which BOTH the cation and the anion are complex ions — and here they are, cobalt in one and chromium in the other. The isomers differ by EXCHANGING the ligands between the two coordination spheres.

In the first compound the ammines are on cobalt and the cyanides on chromium; in the second they have swapped, the ammines going to chromium and the cyanides to cobalt. Every atom is the same; only which metal holds which set of ligands differs.

The other three would each need something absent here. Linkage isomerism needs an AMBIDENTATE ligand; ammonia and cyanide as normally written bind one way each. Hydrate isomerism needs WATER, able to sit inside the sphere or outside as water of crystallisation. Ionization isomerism needs a counter ion to exchange with a ligand, and neither compound has a simple counter ion at all.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
The product formed in the reaction :
A cyclohexane ring bearing a ring \(\mathrm{C=O}\) and, three ring carbons away, a \(\mathrm{-COOC_2H_5}\) group \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaBH_4}}\)
is

options.label: D
options.text: the ring bearing only \(\mathrm{-COOC_2H_5}\), with no oxygen on the ring

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the reactant and ALL FOUR options are drawn cyclohexane rings; the stem names no compound. Reactant: a ring with =O at one carbon and —COOC2H5 three ring carbons away, over an NaBH4 arrow. Options: (a) HO— and —COOC2H5; (b) =O and —CH2OH; (c) HO— and —CH2OH; (d) a bare ring bearing only —COOC2H5. The whole reaction-plus-options block occupies the lower third of page idx 4 and must be attached as a crop. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The product is the ring bearing \(-\mathrm{OH}\) and the ester group unchanged.

Sodium borohydride is a MILD and SELECTIVE reducing agent. It reduces ALDEHYDES and KETONES to alcohols, but it does NOT touch esters, carboxylic acids or amides.

The reason is electronic. An ester's carbonyl carbon is already relieved of much of its positive charge by the neighbouring \(-\mathrm{OR}\) oxygen, which donates a lone pair into the group by resonance. A ketone's carbonyl carbon has no such donor and remains strongly electrophilic, so the hydride attacks it and leaves the ester alone.

Applied here, the ring ketone becomes a secondary alcohol while the \(-\mathrm{COOC_2H_5}\) group survives untouched.

Lithium aluminium hydride would NOT have been selective: it reduces both groups, and the answer would then have been the ring carrying a hydroxyl AND a primary alcohol in place of the ester. Choosing between the two hydrides is the point of the question.

rows.stem: The action of nitrous acid on ethylamine gives mainly :
rows.solution:
The main product is ETHYL ALCOHOL.

Nitrous acid diazotises the primary amine, but an ALIPHATIC diazonium salt is extremely unstable — it decomposes as fast as it forms, even at \(0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), losing nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{C_2H_5N_2^+Cl^-}] \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The carbocation left behind picks up water from the solution, and the product is the alcohol. Brisk effervescence of nitrogen is the visible sign, and measuring that gas is the basis of the Van Slyke method for estimating amino acids.

The contrast with an AROMATIC amine is the lesson. A benzenediazonium salt is stable at \(0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), because the ring delocalises the positive charge, and it can be kept and used to make a whole family of substituted benzenes. No aliphatic diazonium salt can be isolated at all.

rows.stem: The number of faradays passed through a solution of \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) to produce 1 mol of Cu and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) will be :
rows.solution:
TWO faradays are required.

One faraday is the charge carried by one mole of electrons, so count the electrons the cathode reaction needs. Copper is deposited from its \(+2\) ion:
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\)

One mole of copper therefore needs TWO moles of electrons — 2 faradays, about 193000 coulombs.

The oxygen needs no separate charge. Whatever electrons arrive at the cathode must leave from the anode, and the same 2 faradays liberate oxygen there from water:
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4e^-\)

Since that reaction needs 4 faradays per mole of oxygen, 2 faradays give HALF a mole of it — the amount produced alongside one mole of copper. Adding a further 2 faradays for the oxygen would be double counting, which is the trap in the question.

rows.stem: If the initial concentration is reduced to \(\frac{1}{4}\)th in a zero order reaction, then the time taken for half the reaction to complete :
rows.solution:
The time REDUCES TO ONE-FOURTH.

For a zero order reaction the half-life depends on the starting concentration directly:
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2k}\)

So the two are PROPORTIONAL, and reducing \([\mathrm{R}]_0\) to a quarter reduces \(t_{1/2}\) to a quarter as well.

The reason is easy to see without algebra. A zero order reaction proceeds at a CONSTANT rate whatever the concentration — the rate is simply \(k\). With only a quarter as much material to start with, half of it is a quarter as much again, and at an unchanged rate that takes a quarter of the time.

Contrast FIRST order, where the half-life does not depend on the starting concentration at all, so the answer there would have been "remains the same".

rows.stem: On hydrolysis, which of the following carbohydrates gives glucose and fructose ?
rows.solution:
SUCROSE gives glucose and fructose on hydrolysis.

Sucrose is a DISACCHARIDE built from one \(\alpha\)-glucose unit and one \(\beta\)-fructose unit, joined through their anomeric carbons:
\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} + \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

The other options each give something different. STARCH and MALTOSE give only glucose, both being built from glucose alone; LACTOSE gives glucose and GALACTOSE.

Sucrose has a further distinction worth knowing. Because BOTH anomeric carbons are used in the linkage, neither ring can open, so sucrose is a NON-REDUCING sugar — it does not respond to Tollens' or Fehling's reagents, while maltose and lactose do.

The hydrolysis is also called INVERSION: sucrose is dextrorotatory, but the mixture produced is laevorotatory, fructose rotating more strongly to the left than glucose does to the right.

rows.stem: The deficiency of which of the following vitamins causes Scurvy ?
rows.solution:
Scurvy is caused by a deficiency of VITAMIN C, ascorbic acid.

Its symptoms are bleeding gums, loose teeth and wounds that will not heal — all of them failures of CONNECTIVE TISSUE, because vitamin C is needed to make collagen.

The disease is the classic one of long sea voyages, and the reason is the vitamin's solubility. Vitamin C is WATER SOLUBLE, so the body excretes any excess in the urine and stores no reserve; it must be supplied regularly, and a few weeks without fresh fruit or vegetables is enough.

The other options belong elsewhere: vitamin A deficiency gives night blindness, \(\mathrm{B_6}\) gives convulsions, and \(\mathrm{B_{12}}\) gives pernicious anaemia.

rows.stem:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{2.\ H_3O^{+}}]{\mathrm{1.\ CrO_2Cl_2/CS_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)
This reaction is known as :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — both compounds in the printed equation are DRAWN, not named: a benzene ring bearing —CH3 on the left and a benzene ring bearing —CHO on the right, joined by the printed reagent arrow. The stem above renders them as the molecular formulas the drawings show, which is faithful and gives nothing away — the four options are NAMED reactions, so the discrimination rests on knowing the reagent. The printed equation block should still be attached as the crop. Page idx 6, lower half.
rows.solution:
This is the ETARD REACTION.

Chromyl chloride in carbon disulphide attacks the methyl side chain of toluene, forming a brown chromium COMPLEX that precipitates out. Hydrolysis of that complex releases the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}/\mathrm{CS_2}} \text{brown complex} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)

The value of the method is that it STOPS at the aldehyde. Toluene oxidised by permanganate or dichromate goes straight through to benzoic acid, because the aldehyde is more easily oxidised than the hydrocarbon it came from. Trapping it as an inert complex protects it until the oxidising agent has been removed.

The other three named reactions do quite different things: Cannizzaro disproportionates an aldehyde lacking an \(\alpha\) hydrogen, Rosenmund reduces an acyl chloride to an aldehyde, and the aldol joins two carbonyl compounds.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: In which of the following does the central atom exhibit an oxidation state of +4 ?
rows.solution:
Platinum is \(+4\) in \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\).

Let the ligand charges and the overall charge fix the metal's in each case.

Ethane-1,2-diamine is NEUTRAL and the two chlorido ligands give \(-2\); against an overall charge of \(+2\), platinum must be \(+4\). That is the answer.

The other platinum complex is the trap. In \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\) the ammines are neutral and the two chlorides give \(-2\), but the whole complex is NEUTRAL, so platinum is only \(+2\) — the same metal, the same two chlorides, a different state. That compound is cisplatin, the anticancer drug.

In \(\mathrm{K_2[Ni(CN)_4]}\) two potassiums make the complex ion \(2-\), and four cyanides give \(-4\), so nickel is \(+2\). In \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}\) ammonia is neutral, so copper simply carries the \(+2\).

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : When glucose is added to water, an elevation in boiling point is observed.
Reason (R) : The lowering of vapour pressure causes elevation in the boiling point.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Glucose is a non-volatile solute, so adding it to water does raise the boiling point — the Assertion holds. Being a non-electrolyte, glucose contributes one particle per molecule, so the effect is smaller than an equal amount of salt would give, but it is real.

The Reason states the mechanism correctly. A liquid boils at the temperature where its vapour pressure equals the atmospheric pressure. Adding a non-volatile solute LOWERS the vapour pressure at every temperature, so the liquid must be heated FURTHER before its vapour pressure reaches that mark.

So the elevation is not a separate phenomenon standing beside the lowering of vapour pressure; it is a DIRECT CONSEQUENCE of it. The same lowering explains the depression of freezing point in the other direction, which is why the colligative properties are treated as one family.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) for weak electrolytes shows a sharp increase when the electrolytic solution is diluted.
Reason (R) : For weak electrolytes, degree of dissociation decreases with dilution of solution.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

The molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte does rise sharply on dilution — the Assertion is correct.

But the Reason has the direction of dissociation backwards. The degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte INCREASES with dilution, it does not decrease. Dilution shifts the ionisation equilibrium towards MORE ions, which is Ostwald's dilution law, and at infinite dilution a weak electrolyte approaches complete dissociation.

That increase is precisely why the Assertion holds: molar conductivity counts the conductance furnished by one MOLE of electrolyte, and more of that mole is now ionised, so the value climbs steeply.

Corrected, the Reason would have explained the Assertion exactly. As written it contradicts it, since fewer ions would mean a FALLING molar conductivity.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Manganese shows the highest oxidation state of +7 in 3d series.
Reason (R) : Transition metals show variable oxidation states.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Manganese does show \(+7\), the highest oxidation state in the 3d series, in the permanganate ion. And transition metals do show variable oxidation states, as a general fact about the block.

But the general fact does not explain the PARTICULAR one. It says nothing about why MANGANESE should be the element that reaches furthest, and it applies equally to chromium and iron, which do not.

The explanation the Reason would have had to give is manganese's electron count. Its configuration is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\), so it has FIVE UNPAIRED d electrons plus TWO \(4s\) electrons — seven in all, and every one of them available for bonding. No other element of the series has as many, because from iron onwards the d electrons begin to pair up and become less available.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following coordination entities :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_3(H_2O)_3]Cl_3}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{K_3[Al(C_2O_4)_3]}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The three ammine and three aqua ligands are all neutral, and three chlorides sit outside, so chromium must be \(+3\).

Ligands are named in ALPHABETICAL order regardless of charge, and "ammine" precedes "aqua":
TRIAMMINETRIAQUACHROMIUM(III) CHLORIDE

(b) Here the complex is the ANION, so its name takes the suffix \(-\mathrm{ATE}\), and the metal's Latin-derived stem is used where one exists. Aluminium has none, so the name is simply "aluminate".

Three oxalate ligands give \(-6\) against three potassiums outside contributing \(+3\), so the complex ion is \(3-\) and aluminium is \(+3\):
POTASSIUM TRIOXALATOALUMINATE(III)

The cation is named first and written as a separate word, exactly as in an ordinary salt.

rows.stem:
Which of the following is an appropriate set of reactants for the preparation of 1-methoxy-4-nitrobenzene and why ?
(a) Sodium 4-nitrophenoxide \(+\ \mathrm{CH_3Br}\)
(b) 4-Bromonitrobenzene \(+\ \mathrm{CH_3ONa}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — both reactant sets are DRAWN, not named: (a) is a benzene ring bearing —ONa at the top and —NO2 para to it, plus CH3Br; (b) is a benzene ring bearing —Br at the top and —NO2 para to it, plus CH3ONa. The stem above names them in words (sodium 4-nitrophenoxide, 4-bromonitrobenzene), which is a lossless reading of the drawings and gives nothing away — the question asks WHY one set works, which naming does not answer, and the marking scheme itself names the second reagent set 'p-nitrobromobenzene'. The printed reactant block should still be attached as the crop. Page idx 12, upper third.
rows.solution:
The appropriate set is SODIUM 4-NITROPHENOXIDE with BROMOMETHANE.

This is the WILLIAMSON SYNTHESIS, in which an alkoxide or phenoxide displaces halide from an alkyl halide by an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) mechanism:
\(\mathrm{p\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}ONa} + \mathrm{CH_3Br} \longrightarrow \mathrm{p\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{NaBr}\)

It works because bromomethane is a PRIMARY halide, with its carbon fully open to backside attack.

The other combination FAILS, because 4-bromonitrobenzene is an ARYL halide. Its carbon-bromine bond has partial DOUBLE BOND character, the halogen's lone pair being delocalised into the ring, so the bond is shorter and stronger than in an alkyl halide. The ring carbon is also \(sp^2\) and shielded by the \(\pi\) cloud, so a nucleophile cannot approach from behind.

The general rule follows: in planning a Williamson synthesis, put the bulk on the ALKOXIDE and keep the HALIDE primary. An aryl or tertiary halide gives no ether — the aryl one gives no reaction, and the tertiary one gives an alkene instead.
